paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: A large igneous province is an extremely large build-up of igneous rock. It arises when magma travels through the crust towards the surface. Some of the rock is intrusive, in the form of sills and dikes, and some is extrusive, as lava flows and tephra deposits. Most of these provinces are made of basalt, though some also hold large volumes of rhyolite.

paragraphs.heading: How big and how fast
paragraphs.text: When it forms, a province often covers a few million square kilometers and has a volume on the order of 1 million cubic kilometers. In most cases the bulk of a basaltic province is put in place in less than 1 million years. These are short-lived events that pile up volcanic and intrusive rock quickly and in high volume. One puzzle is how such enormous amounts of basaltic magma can form and erupt in so short a time, at rates up to an order of magnitude greater than those of mid-ocean ridge basalts.

paragraphs.heading: Where the magma comes from
paragraphs.text: The source of these provinces has been explained in more than one way. Their formation is put down variously to mantle plumes, to processes tied to plate tectonics, or to meteorite impacts. Mantle plumes are hot material that rises from lower levels of the mantle. Hot material coming up in a plume can spread outward in all directions beneath a tectonic plate and cause regions of uplift. These rising plumes play an important part in forming the provinces.

paragraphs.heading: Unlike ordinary volcanism
paragraphs.text: The great bulk of Earth's volcanism is explained by plate-tectonic processes, and most volcanic activity is tied to subduction zones or mid-oceanic ridges. Large igneous provinces are fundamentally different from any volcano or volcanic system active today. Basalt sea floors and the other products of 'normal' plate tectonics were left out of the definition.

paragraphs.heading: Whole and broken provinces
paragraphs.text: Some provinces are still in one piece, such as the basaltic Deccan Traps in India. Others have been broken up and carried apart by plate movements. The Central Atlantic magmatic province is one of these. Parts of it are now found in Brazil, eastern North America and northwestern Africa.

paragraphs.heading: Extinctions and climate
paragraphs.text: The formation of some provinces in the past 500 million years coincides in time with mass extinctions and rapid changes in climate. Michael Rampino and Richard Stothers cite 11 separate flood basalt episodes in the past 250 million years that coincided with mass extinctions. In the geological record, these provinces mark major changes in the hydrosphere and atmosphere, which led to major climate shifts and maybe to mass extinctions of species. Some of those changes were related to a rapid release of greenhouse gases from the lithosphere into the atmosphere. These past cases may be used to understand environmental change now and in the future.

paragraphs.heading: Metals and minerals
paragraphs.text: Studying these provinces also has economic implications. Economic concentrations of copper–nickel and iron are associated with them. They are linked as well to the forming of major mineral provinces. These include deposits of platinum group elements and, in the silicic provinces, silver and gold deposits. Titanium and vanadium deposits are found with them too.
